Our picks:
the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus is the best small power station for most campers because it has twice the output of its rivals and can grow from 286 Wh to 858 Wh. The Anker SOLIX C300X offers the most outlets, a 10 ms UPS and a 5-year warranty. The Jackery Explorer 300 Plus is the lightest at 8.27 lb. If you car camp with a 12 V fridge or stay out for several days, step up to the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 (1,024 Wh).

What matters in a camping power station
Weight versus capacity: around 300 Wh covers phones, lights and a laptop for a weekend at under 11 lb; 1 kWh units weigh about 25 lb.
USB-C power: most camping gear charges by USB-C, which is more efficient than the AC outlet. Look for at least one 100 W port.
A 12 V car outlet: for compressor coolers, tire inflators and CPAP DC converters.
Solar input: the real key to staying out longer than a weekend.
Quiet operation: it may sit inside your tent.
LiFePO4 chemistry: thousands of cycles instead of hundreds; see LiFePO4 vs lithium-ion.

Estimates use 85% usable capacity, plus about 10 W of inverter overhead for AC loads. Cooler consumption varies a lot with outside temperature and how often you open it; check your model’s rating.
1. EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus: best overall for camping

The RIVER 3 Plus gives you the most flexibility in a small package: 600 W of output, double the Anker and Jackery picks, plus quiet sub-30 dB operation, a one-hour wall recharge, up to 220 W of solar and a UPS under 10 ms. Stack EcoFlow’s extra battery underneath later and it grows to 858 Wh, enough for a 12 V cooler over a long weekend.

Choose it if: you want room to grow and enough output for a small blender or electric blanket.
Skip it if: every ounce counts; it’s the heaviest of the small picks.

Full details: EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus review.

2. Anker SOLIX C300X: most ports and longest warranty

The C300X packs 8 ports into a compact, upright body: 3 AC outlets, 3 USB-C (including two 140 W), a USB-A port and a car socket, plus a built-in ambient light with an SOS mode. It has a 10 ms UPS, a rated noise level of 25 dB, a 288 Wh LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,000+ cycles to 80% and a 5-year warranty. Solar input tops out at 100 W, about 3.2 hours to refill with one 100 W panel in good sun.

Choose it if: you charge lots of USB-C gear (laptops, cameras, drones) and value a long warranty.
Skip it if: you need more than 300 W from the AC outlets.
3. Jackery Explorer 300 Plus: lightest option

At 8.27 lb and about the size of a lunchbox, the Explorer 300 Plus fits in a backpack. It has a 288 Wh LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,000 cycles to 80%, one 300 W AC outlet (600 W peak), a 100 W USB-C port that works for both charging and output, a second USB-C, a USB-A and a car port, plus app control. It charges from the wall in about 2 hours, or from a 100 W solar panel through USB-C.

Choose it if: you hike to your campsite or have very limited space.
Skip it if: you need more than one AC device at a time.
4. BLUETTI Elite 100 V2: best for car camping and longer trips

If you drive to your campsite, a 1 kWh unit opens up much more: running a 12 V fridge for nearly two days, boiling water with an electric kettle, or powering a CPAP for several nights. The Elite 100 V2 offers 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W of output (3,600 W surge), 11 ports, up to 1,000 W of solar input, a 10 ms UPS and a rated noise level of 30 dB or less, all at 25.3 lb in a relatively compact body. BLUETTI says it charges to 80% in about 45 minutes.

Choose it if: you car camp, overland or live in a van.
Skip it if: you need to carry it more than a short distance.

Compare it with its closest rival in BLUETTI vs EcoFlow.

Living on the road or camping in an RV? Charging while you drive and RV connections matter more than size there; see our best power stations for van life and RV.

Camping tips to get more from your battery
Charge by USB-C when you can: it skips the inverter and wastes less energy than plugging a charger into the AC outlet.
Turn off the AC outlets when you aren’t using them; the inverter uses power just by being on.
Keep it in the shade in summer and inside the tent or car on cold nights. Batteries shouldn’t be charged below 32°F.
Top up while driving between campsites through the car outlet.

Need to stay warm on battery? An electric blanket uses about 60–110 W, a fraction of a space heater. See can a power station run an electric blanket for runtimes by battery size.

Frequently asked questions
Can a small power station run a coffee maker?

Usually not. Most drip coffee makers and kettles draw 800–1,500 W, beyond the 300–600 W small units provide. For hot drinks at camp, a 1 kWh unit like the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 or a camp stove is the practical choice.

Is it safe to use a power station inside a tent?
The bottom line

For most campers, a small LiFePO4 unit around 300 Wh is plenty. Pick the EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus if you want room to grow, the Anker SOLIX C300X for ports and warranty, or the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus if every pound counts. For car camping with a fridge, go straight to the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2.

 We have also highlighted exceptional alternatives from Jackery, Bluetti, Anker, and DJI, with DJI serving up tailored power solutions for creators needing on-the-go drone and camera charging.

In our own tests, we found it easily kept up charging three computers, a camera, drone, and lighting for the day. When we hooked up a MacBook Pro, it stayed fully charged with almost a continuous 100W power draw for six hours.
 We were delighted with the number of ports on offer - three AC sockets, one USB-A and two USB-C ports, and a car outlet - letting you power up a full suite of devices and appliances at once.  It's aimed at campers, road-trippers, and travelers, and when we took this out on vacation to the cabin, we could see why.  Battery capacity 
Power station battery capacity is measured in Watt Hours (Wh) - or 1 watt of energy used per hour. The higher the number, the more battery capacity the unit has, the longer it lasts without requiring a recharge. To give you an idea of the power a unit has, an iPhone 17 Pro Max has a battery capacity of 20Wh; the cheapest and smallest portable power station in this guide has a capacity of 245Wh.
 Output 
Output measures the total continuous power supply a unit can deliver, and is measured in Watts (W). Small devices like a laptop and coolers tends to need around 60 to 100W of continuous power whereas appliances like fridges can need up to around 800W. So, a large portable power station with a higher output is best for powering large devices, or more devices at once.
 Input 
Portable power stations are usually charged via the mains - it's quick and efficient, especially for higher-capacity units. Many also let you charge the device from the car using a 12V cigarette lighter socket - ideal for those living the van life or in the RV. You can recharge some devices using solar panels, too.
 Solar 
Every portable power station I've selected for this guide have solar charging capabilities for off-grid power supply, but not every unit you can buy does. The solar panels can come bundled with the unit or bought separately. Smaller power stations will have a lower maximum solar input, making them slower to charge.
 UPS 
Uninterrupted Power Supply (UPS) is essential for ensuring reliable and continuous power even during black-outs. If you're using your unit for devices like routers or fridges, it's. Effectively, a UPS-enabled power station will step in during a power outage to continue charging or powering connected devices. Times vary, and while we're talking a matter of milliseconds, if it's a 'mission-critical' device, then select one with a faster switchover time.
 High surge wattage 
 This is especially important if you're using a portable power station on a job-site, as some tools, like circular saws, draw a huge amount of power at once. So, a unit with a high surge wattage (or high surge rating) prevents the machinery from tripping out the unit.
 Size & weight 
"Portable" isn't one size fits all. My team and I have reviewed everything from compact and handheld units to massive power stations that have built in wheels or need a trolley to move them. Depending on how and where you'll be using the unit, you'll want check the dimensions. As you'd expect, the higher the battery capacity, the heavier the power station will be.
 Ports 
Port selection is always worth checking. Portable power stations almost always include USB-C and USB-A ports, as well as mains outlets. However, larger units will usually have a higher number of ports as there's extra space for them, and the unit holds more power to charge more devices. Some go beyond this - for example, DJI's products include an SDC port for charging DJI drones on the go.
 Best portable power stations: FAQs 
 Are portable power stations worth it?
 Yes, but it depends on how often you use it and how many devices you're charging. There are a lot of models on the market, and the best portable power stations can handle everything from charging mobile devices and laptops to powering appliances and even EVs. If your needs are simple, you can pick up a good portable power station for around $200.
If you like going to campsites that have a power hookup they're not worth it as connecting to mains doesn't cost that much compared to a power station. For longer periods off-grid a generator is still, for me, the better option but for short weekend trips where you cannot get a power source these can completely change the weekend for the better if you want to keep using your tech or use electric-powered camping gadgets.
 What is the difference between a portable power station and a generator?
 Generally speaking, a portable power station is charged and outputs electricity. Generators tend to refer to units that use fuel like gasoline to generate energy and power. 
 Both can be used for back-up purposes, and both have different pros and cons. 
 Power stations are quieter, cleaner and more eco-friendly. However, their battery capacity can be low, and if it runs out of charge during a power-cut, you'd best hope it has built-in solar panels to re-charge. 
 Power generators are ideal for running heavy appliances, as they have a higher capacity, and isn't reliant on electricity, making it perfect for a back-up solution. 
 How many years do portable power stations last?
 A portable power station's lifespan depends on usage frequency and battery chemistry, but most last between 5 and 10 years with regular use. Like a phone or laptop battery, its capacity gradually degrades over time until it can no longer hold a full charge.
 THere are several key factors influence a portable power station's longevity: 
 The first is the battery type; models with Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries often last up to 10 years (3,000+ full charge cycles), while standard Lithium-ion (NMC) models usually last 3 to 5 years (500 to 1,000 cycles) before capacity drops to 80%. 
 The second and third factors, which we've combines, depends on a station's usage and storage; frequent deep discharges, exposure to extreme temperatures, and storing the unit fully empty accelerate battery degradation all affect its lifespan.
 How many Watt Hours do I need?
 Start by listing every device or appliance you want to power. For anything you'll run continuously — a fridge, a router, a lamp — multiply its wattage by the number of hours you need it running. For devices you'll charge and then use, like a phone or laptop, find the battery capacity in Wh (usually on the device label or manufacturer's website) and multiply that by the number of times you want to charge it.
 Add all those figures together and that's your minimum capacity requirement.
 It's worth adding a 20–30% buffer on top of that figure. Real-world capacity is affected by temperature, battery age, and the startup surge that motors and compressors draw when they first switch on.
 What can you run on a portable power station?
 So long as your portable power station has the right ports and enough capacity, it can run a massive range of devices, including phones, laptops, and desktops. 
 Higher capacity units will also let you power large home appliances and charge electric vehicles. 
 Check which ports your preferred model has, including USB Type-A and Type-C, AC and mains sockets.
 How long can you run a portable power station?
 It all depends on the power station and the device or devices you're charging. As a general rule of thumb, to figure out how long your portable power station can run, divide battery capacity (Wh) by power drawn by the device (W). 
 What is UPS and why do I need it?
 UPS stands for Uninterrupted Power Supply, and it’s a really important feature if you’re powering devices like routers and household appliances like fridges, or working on-site and need reliability. If you experience a power outage, the portable power station will automatically and seamlessly continue charge your devices without dropping the supply. 
 How we test the best portable power stations 
 Our team of expert reviewers have hand-tested a range of outdoor-ready equipment, including the best rugged smartphones , the best rugged laptops , and the best rugged tablets for working out in the field. We've even tested out the best rugged hard drives . So, we know what to look for when it comes to technology for rural locations and hostile environments.
 We test the best portable power stations on volume, weight, battery chemistry, and additional feature sets. Before writing any review, we try to fully understand the unit to describe each device's pros and cons best and accurately compare them. Part of this process is through benchmark tests, part is through daily use, and part is through simulated or real scenarios.
 As the main function of these devices is to be batteries, we test charge and discharge cycles on every unit. First and foremost, this is the most important feature of the portable power stations we test. If they cannot meet our standard here or do not come near what the other portable power stations in this guide are capable of, we will most likely not include them.
 Next, we push the power stations to their limits and beyond. We intentionally exceed the maximum power allowed on each generator, then observe and note the recovery from the over-power protection. This helps us promote safe power stations for you and your family.
 To ensure reliability, these tests are designed to learn the features, the downfalls, and the limits of the power stations tested by our subject matter experts.

 What to Look for When Buying a Camping Power Station
 Capacity: How Many Watt-Hours Do You Actually Need?
 Most buyers over-spec on capacity. A realistic camping load calculation:
 CPAP (non-heated): ~30–60 Wh per night
 Mini 12V fridge (running): ~40–60 Wh per hour
 Laptop (MacBook Pro 14"): ~20–30 Wh per charge
 Smartphone: ~10–15 Wh per charge
 LED camp lights: ~5–15 Wh per evening
 A two-night weekend car camping trip with a fridge, CPAP, phones, and laptop rarely exceeds 600–800 Wh of actual draw. The 1,000 Wh class gives you a comfortable buffer with solar recharging. The 2,000 Wh class is for extended trips, large groups, or van builds.
 Battery Chemistry: LFP vs. NMC
 LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries run 2,500–3,500 cycles before significant degradation. NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) batteries typically rate 500–1,000 cycles. For camping gear used 20–30 times per year, NMC can still last several years — but LFP is the better long-term value if the price is comparable.
 Spec sheets and long-term user feedback consistently point to LFP as the better choice for anyone planning to keep a unit more than three or four seasons.
 Solar Input: Don't Ignore the Ceiling
 A unit that accepts 500W of solar charges roughly twice as fast as one capped at 200W — important if you're off-grid for more than a day. EcoFlow and Bluetti's upper-tier units have the highest solar input ceilings; Jackery and Goal Zero tend to run lower, sometimes requiring proprietary panel ecosystems. If solar recharging is part of your setup, check our solar generator guide for pairing recommendations.
 Weight vs. Capacity Tradeoff
 There is no free lunch here. More watt-hours means more weight — budget roughly 1–1.5 kg per 100 Wh as a rough benchmark for this class. Units claiming to beat that ratio significantly usually compromise somewhere else (output, cycle life, or build quality).
 Picking for Tailgating, RV, and Base Camp
 Camping isn't the only reason to buy one of these, and the right pick shifts with the use case:
 Tailgating. Tailgating is short — a few hours — but often higher-draw than camping: a blender, an electric griddle or grill, a TV, and speakers, not just phone charging. So continuous output matters more than capacity here. The 800W units (Anker SOLIX C800, EcoFlow River 2 Pro) comfortably run a TV, speakers, lights, and a mini fridge, but they'll trip the moment you hit a blender or griddle. For party appliances, step up to the EcoFlow Delta 2 (1,800W) or Bluetti AC200P (2,000W) , which handle a blender, small griddle, or coffee maker. Weight is a non-issue — you're lifting it out of a truck bed, not hiking — so the Delta 2 is the sweet spot for most tailgaters.
 RV. Continuous fridge draw plus occasional higher loads, with solar to top up over multi-day trips. The EcoFlow Delta 2 (expandable, 500W solar) or Bluetti AC200P (700W solar, higher capacity) fit best; the Bluetti's higher solar ceiling and capacity suit longer stays without hookups.
 Group base camp. Multi-day, multi-person — capacity wins. The Bluetti AC200P's 2,000 Wh is the logical pick; treat it as a stationary unit you place and leave.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 How many watt-hours do I need for a camping weekend? 
For a solo or couple car camping trip — running a mini fridge, charging phones and a laptop, and powering LED lights — 500–800 Wh covers most two-night trips with moderate solar top-up. If you add a CPAP or multiple people, step up to the 1,000 Wh class.
 Can I run a CPAP machine off a portable power station? 
Yes — most CPAP machines without a heated humidifier draw 30–60W and consume 60–120 Wh per eight-hour night. A 500 Wh unit can run a CPAP for two to four nights depending on settings. Heated humidifiers increase draw significantly; disable them to extend runtime.
 What's the difference between a solar generator and a portable power station? 
A "solar generator" is a marketing term for a portable power station sold with or designed for solar panels. There's no technical difference — the unit itself is a portable power station. Bundled solar panel kits are often poor value per watt compared to buying panels separately.
 Is LFP worth the extra cost over NMC chemistry? 
In most cases, yes — but it depends on usage frequency. If you camp 20+ times per year and plan to keep the unit five or more years, LFP's 3,000+ cycle life is worth the premium. Occasional campers (five to ten trips per year) are unlikely to hit NMC's cycle limit within a reasonable ownership window.
 Can I charge a portable power station while using it? 
Most units support simultaneous charge-and-discharge (sometimes called "pass-through charging"), including all seven products in this guide. Check the manual for any specific caveats — some units throttle output or charging speed in passthrough mode.
 Can a power station run tailgating gear like a blender or electric griddle? 
Only the higher-output units. A blender or electric griddle pulls roughly 800–1,500W, which exceeds the 300–800W continuous ceiling on the smaller picks here — they'll fault. The EcoFlow Delta 2 (1,800W) and Bluetti AC200P (2,000W) handle those loads; the 800W units (Anker SOLIX C800, EcoFlow River 2 Pro) are fine for a TV, speakers, lights, and a mini fridge, but not high-draw cooking appliances. For tailgating, size by output wattage first, capacity second.
 Are these units airline-safe? 
Most portable power stations exceed airline lithium battery limits (100 Wh for carry-on; up to 160 Wh with airline approval). A 1,000 Wh unit is not allowed on commercial flights in any class. For air travel, goal zero sherpa-class small units or dedicated travel battery banks are your options.
 Conclusion: The Best Portable Power Station for Camping
 For most car campers, the EcoFlow Delta 2 is the clearest recommendation — 1,024 Wh, LFP chemistry, fast charging, and enough output to run real appliances at a price that's competitive in its class. If budget is the priority and 800W AC is enough, the EcoFlow River 2 Pro is the best value per watt-hour in this guide.
 Backpackers and ultralight campers should look at the Jackery Explorer 300 Plus — it's the only option here sized for human-powered travel. And if you're building out a van or base camp that needs multi-day, multi-person power, the Bluetti AC200P is the logical step up — just accept that it lives in your vehicle, not in your hand.
 The best portable power station for camping isn't the one with the most watt-hours. It's the one that matches your actual load, fits in your vehicle, and lasts long enough to justify the investment.

 Size the battery to your trip, not to the biggest number on the box. Most camping setups fall into one of three groups.

 Phones, lights, a fan, a camera. Small loads, short trips.

 Camping Power Tips That Stretch Your Battery 
 Use DC for 12V gear
 Run a 12V fridge or a CPAP from the car or DC outlet instead of the AC outlets. It skips the inverter and its losses.
 Charge while you drive
 Every pick here recharges from a car socket. A few hours on the road puts energy back before the next night.
 Keep it cool and dry
 Leave the station in the shade and out of the rain. Heat slows charging and wears the battery.
 Mind the cold

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What is the best portable power station for camping? 
 For most campers, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 : 1,024Wh runs a 12V fridge for a long weekend, 2,000W handles camp cooking, and it recharges in 49 minutes from the wall or 1.8 hours from 600W of solar. If weight matters more, the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Pro (18.2 lb) or the RIVER 3 Plus (10.4 lb) are easier to carry. For CPAP users, the BLUETTI AC180 is our pick.
 What size power station do I need for camping? 
 For a weekend of phones, lights and a fan, 300 to 600Wh is enough. Add a 12V fridge or cooler and you want 700 to 1,200Wh. For a family, a multi-day trip or a nightly CPAP, look at 1,000 to 2,000Wh. Check your own gear with the power station calculator .
 How long will a power station run a camping fridge? 
 A 12V camping fridge averaging 45W runs about 5.5 hours on a 286Wh unit, about 15 hours on 768Wh, about 19 to 22 hours on a 1kWh-class unit and about 39 hours on 2,042Wh. Running the fridge from the 12V outlet rather than AC stretches that further, and so does keeping the fridge out of the sun. See our guide to camping fans and coolers .
 Can I run a CPAP machine while camping? 
 Yes. A CPAP drawing 40W for 8 hours uses about 320Wh, so a 1kWh-class station covers 2.5 to 3 nights and the 2,042Wh Explorer 2000 v2 about 5.5 nights. A humidifier or heated tube adds significantly to the draw. Running the CPAP on DC through a 12V outlet, as the BLUETTI AC180 allows, avoids inverter losses.
 How many times can a camping power station charge a phone or laptop? 
 Divide the usable capacity (about 85% of the rated watt-hours) by the device battery. Assuming a phone battery of about 15Wh and a laptop battery of about 60Wh, a 288Wh unit gives roughly 16 phone or 4 laptop charges, a 768Wh unit about 43 or 11, a 1,024Wh unit about 58 or 14, and the 2,042Wh Explorer 2000 v2 about 115 or 29.
 Can I run a heater or an electric blanket while camping? 
 A blanket, yes; a space heater, barely. A typical 1,500W space heater would drain a 1,024Wh station in about 35 minutes. A 12V heated blanket drawing around 50W, on the other hand, runs about 17 hours on the same unit. In cold weather, also remember that several of these stations can’t recharge below 32°F.
 Is a solar generator the same as a portable power station? 
 Almost. “Solar generator” is the marketing name for a portable power station sold with solar panels. The station stores and delivers the power; the panels recharge it. You can also buy the station alone and add compatible panels later.
 Can I charge a camping power station from my car? 
 Yes, all seven picks recharge from a 12V car socket. It is slow compared with a wall outlet (EcoFlow quotes about 3.3 hours for the 286Wh RIVER 3 Plus), but a day of driving adds meaningful energy between campsites.

 We tested the best portable power stations. These stood out.
 Don’t be left out in the dark in the next power outage or on your next trip into the great outdoors. 
 By Tony Carrick , Special to Hearst July 27, 2026 
 Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra outside in the rain.
 Stacey L. Nash Portable power stations are essential for keeping your home’s essentials up and running during a power outage. They produce enough juice to keep personal electronics charged, fridges running, and essential medical equipment like CPAP machines working when the power goes out. 
 Unlike a standard home backup system that’s permanently installed, portable power stations are, well, portable. They sit on wheels or are light enough to pick up, so you can use them to provide electricity when camping or RVing off the grid. 
 When it comes to choosing a portable power station or solar generator , you’ve got a lot of options. Portable power stations designed to provide backup power or off-grid power range in capacity from small 1,500-watt-hour (Wh) models for powering a coffee maker, portable fridge, and lights while camping to 4,000Wh beasts that can power a fridge for days or keep other essentials running. We tested several top portable power stations from leading brands to find the best for backup power, whether you’re at home or at the campsite. 
 Best overall: Bluetti Apex 300 Portable Power Station 
 Best value: Anker Solix C2000 
 Best whole-home backup: EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 
 Best for camping: Goal Zero Yeti 1500 Portable Power Station (6th Gen) 
 Best weather-resistant: Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra 
 How we decided on the best portable power stations
 I chose the five top models from some of the best-regarded portable power station brands. Of those five, I tested three in my home. I evaluated each model’s maximum output and capacity, as well as charging time and portability. I started by hooking up multiple high-wattage appliances to each power station, then ran them simultaneously to see if each unit could handle its listed load. I followed by using an electricity usage meter to see how much energy each power station produces under a consistent load. Along with performance, I also considered each power station's portability by moving each one around my home and loading each model into the trunk of my car. 
 For those portable power stations that I did not hand-test, I compared specs and pored through user reviews to make my selections. 
 Best overall: Bluetti Apex 300 Portable Power Station 
 BLUETTI BLUETTI Solar Generator Apex 300 
 $1699.00 at amazon.com 
 Bluetti’s Apex presents a clear departure from standard portable power stations by focusing solely on serving as a backup power source for essential appliances such as refrigerators and medical equipment. The Apex 300 doesn’t bother with USB-C charging ports or DC outlets, instead focusing on a whole-home backup with four AC outputs and one 240-volt output. There are also 30-amp and 50-amp inputs on the side, so I can connect it directly to my RV’s electrical system.
 The Apex 300 also has a high 7,680-watt surge rating, so it can handle appliances and tools that draw a lot of power at startup, including air conditioning units, power tools, and refrigerators. I hooked up a fridge, window air conditioner, and miter saw to the Apex 300 and had no problem running all three at once. 
 Along with impressive output, the Apex 300 also offers far more solar charging capacity than most portable power stations, at 4,000 watts. At that rate, Bluetti says it’s possible to charge it to 80% in just 45 minutes and to full in just over an hour. The Apex 300 also provides 240-volt power at the flip of a switch, so you can use it to power heavy-duty appliances like a well pump or dryer. 
 The Apex 300 also offers several advantages for RVing. While it’s by no means light, it's lighter than most portable power stations in this capacity class. At 84 pounds, I’m still able to carry it short distances and lift it into the bed of my truck on my own.

 Anker Solix’s C2000 offers impressive capacity and charging times in a compact size. 
 Small yet powerful 
 The Anker Solix 2000 offers one of the best power-to-weight ratios we’ve seen out of a portable power station. It has a 2,048Wh capacity yet weighs just 41 pounds. That’s small enough that I can comfortably carry it to the second floor of my home, or even use it for short-term off-shore power for my RV. 
 Anker Solix C2000 review.
 Tony Carrick I tested the Anker Solix 2000 at home, plugging in what I would call essential electronics, including my laptop, router, and TV, followed by a higher-demand appliance, my air fryer. Using each as I normally would, I drew about 75 watts, which is enough for about 24 hours' worth of use. My air fryer has settings that allow it to draw up to 1,800 watts for max crisping. The C2000 had no problem handling these higher watts, though I should note that running 1,800 watts will drain the battery in just over an hour. If you need more juice, the C2000 is expandable to 4,000 Wh. 
 The C2000 has many outputs for its size, including five 120-volt outlets, three USB-C outlets, a USB-A outlet, a car accessory socket, and a 30-amp outlet for RVs. It’s also one of the first power stations we’ve seen with a high-resolution display. 
 Best-in-class charging
 While I love the power-to-weight ratio, what I really like about this power station is how quickly it charges. It took about 45 minutes to reach 80% and about an hour to reach 100%, the fastest recharge time we've seen for any portable power station of this capacity. Most 2,000Wh portable power stations take about 80 minutes to charge. The C2000 also offers a high maximum solar panel input of 800 watts, meaning you can recharge it from zero to 100 in just a few hours of direct sunlight.

 Best whole-home backup:  EcoFlow Delta Pro 3

 Built for home backup
 EcoFlow’s Delta Pro 3’s large capacity and incredible efficiency make it one of the best portable options for whole-home backup. It boasts a whopping 4,000 watts, a surge capacity of up to 6,000 watts, and 4,096Wh with just the base unit. 
 That's enough juice to power their load power stools or window air conditioning units. I attached a coffee maker and an air fryer to the Delta Pro, then ran both at the same time, with a total output pushing 4,000 watts. The Delta Pro 3 operated each simultaneously with no drops in power. The Delta Pro 3 is also one of the most efficient power stations we've tested, recording a whopping 95% efficiency, so very little of its 4,096Wh capacity is lost to the inverter.

 The Delta Pro 3 offers many options for powering it. In addition to its four standard 120-volt outlets, there are two 220-volt outlets, plus a 30-amp RV outlet and USB ports for electronics. This broad range of output options lets you operate a dryer, water pump, or AC unit with the Delta Pro 3. 
 High solar charging capacity
 The Delta Pro 3 also offers some of the highest-capacity solar charging we’ve seen, with two solar panels that total 2,600 watts.  
 The EcoFlow sits on two wheels and has a retractable handle that lets you roll it around like carry-on luggage. While this made moving this 113-pound beast around manageable, it’s not something you’ll lift into the back of the truck without help and a fair amount of strength.

 The problem with many portable power stations is that they lack the weather resistance to make them a true option for camping and other outdoor activities. That’s not the case with the new Goal Zero Yeti 1500 6G. This portable power station boasts IPX4 weather resistance, which means it can withstand light rain showers and splashes. Unlike other portable power stations with hard plastic housings, the Yeti 1500 6G has an aluminum case and covers that protect its outlets when it’s not in use, inspiring confidence in its durability. The Goal Zero Yeti 1500 G has even been vibration-tested, so it can withstand off-road use. 
 In terms of power output, the Yeti can deliver up to 2,000 watts of continuous power with a 3,600-watt surge capacity. It has 1,500 Wh of total capacity and charges quickly, reaching 80% in under an hour and 100% in a little over an hour. The Yeti 1,500 6G is also equipped to handle up to 900 watts of solar power, allowing it to charge off-grid in a couple of hours. While we like how rugged it is, it comes in a bit heavy at 52 pounds. It can also function as a UPC.

 Best weather-resistant: Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra 
 Jackery Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Portable Power Station 
 $1199.00 at amazon.com 
 Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra — our full review here — is one of a new crop of power stations designed to handle the elements. It’s one of the most weather-resistant power stations we’ve seen yet. It has an IP65 rating, which means it’s dustproof and can withstand water projected at it from any direction. Jackery says it can also withstand drops of up to 1 meter. 
 Real-world test: rain, drops, outage. The Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra didn’t flinch.
 Stacey L. Nash The Explorer 1500 Ultra comes with a broad range of ports, including three 120-volt outlets, one USB-A port, two USB-C ports, and a 12-volt car accessory outlet. Along with its 1,800-watt max output, it can also deliver a 3,600-watt surge for up to 5 seconds, which is a lot for a power station of this size. Its total charge time of about 80 minutes is somewhat slow. You’ll find other power stations with similar output that can recharge fully in about half the time. 
 Jackery also does not include a built-in light on the unit, which is something typically found on all of its portable power stations. It’s odd that it chose to forgo that feature in this model, which is designed for outdoor use. It’s an ideal portable power station for camping to throw in the back of a truck bed for a trip to a job site.

 What we don’t like:

 What to consider when looking for a portable power station
 Max output
 A portable power station's maximum output determines the maximum sustained wattage it can deliver and, hence, what you can power with it. When shopping for a power station, look for one with the maximum output to power the electronics and appliances you plan to plug into it. If you’re planning to run a 600-watt fridge and an 800-watt coffee maker simultaneously, then you’ll need a portable power station capable of sustaining more than 1,400 watts.  
 Power stations also have surge power, a higher-wattage output they can sustain for very short periods, typically one to five seconds. Surge output is typically around 50% higher than the power station's standard output. Surge power is helpful for powering appliances and tools that require more power to start, such as a miter saw or a refrigerator. 
 Capacity
 A portable power station’s capacity is listed in watt-hours (Wh) and indicates how much power it can produce before it needs to be recharged; the larger the capacity, the longer it can run. Portable power stations for camping or home backup generally range from around 1,500Wh for short bursts of power to run electronics and appliances to 4,100Wh for the largest models that can run higher-wattage appliances and tools, and a fridge for days. A 4,000Wh power station can run a fridge that uses 1,300Wh per day for three or four days. You can estimate how long a power station will run your electronics or appliances by dividing its capacity by the total wattage of the devices. 
 Durability 
 Portable power stations are designed for use while camping, so they should be able to withstand the elements. Most power stations can withstand splashes of water and humid environments, but they aren’t designed to be left out in the rain or to withstand sustained water sprays, nor will they withstand falls. Portable power stations designed for outdoor use can withstand rain, water spray, and falls of up to a meter.  
 Outputs
 Portable power stations have various output types for use. Most portable power stations have several standard 120-volt outlets, various types of USB outlets, and a 12V car accessory port. Some also have 30-amp ports that let you connect the portable power station directly to your RV, as well as 240-volt outlets for higher-power appliances like dryers. 
 Charging
 Portable power stations can charge in various ways. All portable power stations can recharge via an AC cable. Most can also be recharged via a solar panel. They can typically take between 400 and 2,600 watts of solar panels. Some can also be recharged using an EV charger or by a car’s alternator via a car accessory port. 
 Portable power station FAQs
 How long does it take to charge a portable power station?
 The time it takes to charge a portable power station depends on the power station's capacity and the solar panels' output. To get an estimate, divide the power station's total watt-hours by the solar panels' wattage. A 400-watt solar panel, which actually produces around 300 watts, will take about 210 hours of direct sunlight to fully recharge a 3,000Wh power station. 
 What can I power with a portable power station?
 What you can power with a portable power station depends on its capacity. A 300Wh to 500Wh portable power station is ideal for powering laptops and smartphones. 800Wh to 1,500Wh power stations are large enough to power a coffee maker or mini fridge yet small enough to move around, making them ideal for camping. Larger 2,000Wh to 3,500Wh power stations are ideal for whole-home backup or for powering an RV.

 The fastest way to waste money on a camping power station — or a solar
generator , which is the same product sold with panels — is to buy on capacity
alone. The second fastest is to buy on brand. What actually decides the right
unit for camping is a three-way trade between watt-hours, weight, and whether
you can recharge from the sun.
 Start with the math, not the model # 
 Everything follows from one number: watt-hours per day .
 daily Wh = Σ (device watts × hours used) 
 capacity needed = daily Wh × nights ÷ 0.85 
 The 0.85 is inverter efficiency — a “1,000 Wh” unit delivers roughly 850 Wh at
the AC outlet. Three worked examples:
 Weekend tent trip, no fridge. 
Two phones (10 W × 2 × 2 h = 40 Wh), a lantern (5 W × 6 h = 30 Wh), camera
batteries (30 Wh), a laptop one evening (60 W × 2 h = 120 Wh) — call it
220 Wh/day. Two nights: 440 ÷ 0.85 = 518 Wh . A 1,000 Wh unit is comfortable;
a 300 Wh unit works if you skip the laptop.
 Van weekend with a 12V fridge. 
Fridge (13.5 W average × 24 h = 324 Wh), phones and lights (70 Wh), CPAP on DC
(100 Wh) — 494 Wh/day. Two nights: 988 ÷ 0.85 = 1,162 Wh. This is the
1 kWh class, and it’s why that class is the camping default.
 Five days boondocking. 
Same 494 Wh/day × 5 = 2,470 ÷ 0.85 = 2,906 Wh. No portable unit in this
guide covers that on battery alone. You either move up to the expandable 2 kWh
class and carry panels, or you accept a mid-trip drive to recharge.
 Run your own numbers in the sizing calculator —
it uses exactly this formula.
 Weight is the spec nobody reads # 
 For camping specifically, weight matters more than the spec sheets suggest,
because it decides whether the unit lives in your car or comes to the site.
 Model Capacity Weight Wh per lb 
 EcoFlow RIVER 2 256 Wh 7.7 lbs 33 
 Jackery Explorer 300 Plus 288 Wh 8.3 lbs 35

 EcoFlow DELTA 2 1,024 Wh 27.0 lbs 38 
 EcoFlow DELTA 3 1,024 Wh 27.6 lbs 37 
 Anker SOLIX C1000 1,056 Wh 28.4 lbs 37 
 BLUETTI AC180 1,152 Wh 35.3 lbs 33 
 The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 carries 45 Wh per pound — meaningfully ahead of
everything else in its class. Over a 100-yard carry from the car to a tent
pitch, 23.8 lbs versus 35.3 lbs is the difference between one trip and two.
 The picks # 
 Best overall — Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 # 
 1,070 Wh, 1,500 W continuous, 3,000 W surge, 23.8 lbs, $999 ($0.93/Wh).
 It wins on the spec that matters most for this use case. It’s the lightest
1 kWh-class unit in our database by 3.2 lbs, it carries the most capacity per
pound, and 1,070 Wh covers the standard van-weekend load with headroom.
 The compromises are honest ones: 100 minutes to recharge from the wall (versus
56 for the DELTA 3), only 400 W of solar input, and no expansion battery
option. For a camper who recharges at home between trips, none of those bite.
 Best value — EcoFlow DELTA 3 # 
 1,024 Wh, 1,800 W continuous, 3,600 W surge, 27.6 lbs, $699 ($0.68/Wh).
 The best price per watt-hour in the 1 kWh class, with the longest-lived cell here
(4,000 cycles to 80%) and a 56-minute full recharge. 500 W of solar input beats
the Jackery’s 400 W, and it expands to 5 kWh if your needs grow.
 You pay for that in 3.8 extra pounds. If the unit rides in a van or a truck bed
rather than on your back, take the $300 and the faster charging.
 Best for device-heavy camping — Anker SOLIX C1000 # 
 1,056 Wh, 1,800 W continuous, 28.4 lbs, $999 ($0.95/Wh).
 The reason to pick this one is 600 W of solar input — the highest in the
1 kWh class, and 50% more than the Jackery. If you’re running panels, that’s
the difference between recovering 400 Wh and 600 Wh on a good afternoon. It
also charges from the wall in 58 minutes and has the broadest port selection
here.
 Best budget — EcoFlow RIVER 2 # 
 256 Wh, 300 W continuous, 7.7 lbs, $239 ($0.93/Wh).
 At 7.7 lbs this is the unit you carry without thinking about it, and for
device-only camping it’s genuinely sufficient — 256 Wh is roughly a full
weekend of phones, lights, and camera batteries. A 60-minute recharge is
remarkable at the price.
 Know its limit. The 300 W inverter will not run a compressor fridge, a
kettle, or anything with a heating element. If a fridge is anywhere in your
plans, skip to the 1 kWh class; nothing here bridges that gap.
 When solar stops being optional # 
 Past two nights off-grid, panels change the arithmetic more than a bigger
battery does.
 A 200 W panel array returns roughly 600–800 Wh on a clear day — real-world,
after accounting for angle, temperature derating, and the fact that peak sun
lasts a few hours rather than all day. Treat the panel’s rated wattage as a
best case you’ll rarely hit; 60–70% of rating over a good day is a fair
planning figure.
 That means 200 W of panels roughly covers the 494 Wh/day van-weekend load
indefinitely in summer sun. It does not cover it in a forest, in shoulder
season, or under cloud. Solar extends your trip; it doesn’t guarantee it.
 Match panels to your unit’s maximum solar input — 400 W on the Jackery,
500 W on the DELTA 3, 600 W on the Anker. Exceeding it wastes money; the
charge controller simply caps.
 If you’re buying the panels at the same time as the battery, the bundles the
brands sell as solar generators are the same hardware in one box, and
whether they save money depends entirely on the per-watt price of the panels
inside. We work that out model by model in
 the best solar generator for camping .
 What can you actually run at a campsite? # 
 Capacity decides how long; the inverter decides what at all. This is where the
300 Wh class stops and the 1 kWh class starts:
 Load Watts Runs on 300 W inverter? Wh per use 
 Phone charging 10 W Yes 15–20 Wh 
 LED lantern 5 W Yes 30–50 Wh 
 Laptop 60 W Yes 60–120 Wh 
 Starlink Standard 50–75 W Yes 1,200–1,800 Wh/day 
 CPAP on DC 10–15 W Yes ~100 Wh/night 
 12V fridge 45 W running Marginal — surge may trip it ~324 Wh/day 
 Electric kettle 1,200 W No 40 Wh per boil 
 Induction hob 1,500 W No 250 Wh per meal 
 Coffee maker 900 W No 45 Wh per brew 
 Note how little energy the big loads actually consume — a kettle is 1,200 W but
only for two minutes. The problem is never capacity with cooking appliances,
it’s the inverter’s continuous rating. If you want to boil water, you need a
1,500 W+ inverter, which means the 1 kWh class or above regardless of how few
watt-hours you use.
 The honest advice for most campers: cook on gas and use the battery for
electronics. A camp stove does in three minutes what costs you a quarter of
your battery.
 What we’d skip # 
 Anything with NMC chemistry. The Goal Zero Yeti 1000X is well-built and
rugged, but at $1.32/Wh with older cells and a 9-hour wall recharge, it’s
outclassed by everything above for camping.
 A 2 kWh unit for tent camping. The BLUETTI AC200L and EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max
are excellent, but at 62.4 and 50 lbs they’re car-camping and RV items. Buying
one for a tent site means it stays in the trunk.
 Gas generators , unless you genuinely need to run an air conditioner. They’re
loud enough to annoy every neighbouring site, banned in a growing number of
campgrounds, and can’t run inside a van.
 How do you keep it charged at camp? # 
 Three options, and most people should plan for two of them.
 Charge before you leave. Obvious, but the recharge times differ enough to
change trip planning. The DELTA 3 goes wall-to-full in 56 minutes, the Anker
SOLIX C1000 in 58, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 in 100. If you’re leaving in an
hour, only some of these are ready.
 Charge from the vehicle. Every unit here accepts 12V input from a car
socket, but it’s slow — a typical cigarette-lighter socket delivers about
100 W, so filling a 1 kWh unit takes ten hours of driving. Treat it as topping
up, not charging. Units supporting alternator charging (via a dedicated DC-DC
charger) do far better, and that’s worth checking if you drive between sites.
 Charge from the sun. Covered above — the realistic figure is 60–70% of
rated panel wattage across a good day.
 The practical pattern for a multi-night trip is: leave fully charged, run a
panel during the day, and use the drive between sites as a bonus top-up. Any
one of the three alone tends to disappoint.

RV boondocking without hookups usually means 1,000–2,000 Wh plus solar.

It's worth it if you camp more than two nights off-grid: 200 W of panels can return 600–800 Wh to the battery on a sunny day, which covers a fridge, lights, and device charging. 
 How much does a camping power station weigh? The 1 kWh class runs 23.8–35.3 lbs depending on model, which is the range where weight starts to matter for tent camping. The 300 Wh class is 7.7–8.3 lbs and genuinely portable. Anything in the 2 kWh class is 50 lbs or more and is realistically an RV or car-camping item.

 How many watt-hours you actually need
 Skip the marketing categories and do the arithmetic once. A phone charge is roughly 15Wh, so even a small unit recharges a phone a dozen times. A laptop is 50 to 60Wh per charge. A CPAP runs roughly 50 to 100Wh a night with the humidifier off, and a heated humidifier can triple that. A 12V fridge is the load that changes everything: the fridge plus lights, fans, and device charging typically draws 500 to 900Wh a day.
 Two corrections before you match those numbers to a spec sheet. First, plan on about 85% of rated capacity reaching your gear, because the inverter takes a cut. A 1,024Wh unit delivers roughly 870Wh in practice. Second, capacity only has to bridge the gap between recharges. If you carry enough solar to cover your daily draw, a 1,000Wh unit runs a fridge camp indefinitely; without solar, it runs it for about a day.
 So the sizing answer is short. Phones, lights, and a laptop for a weekend: a 300Wh-class unit. Anything with a fridge or CPAP: 1,000Wh plus solar. A base camp running power tools or a family's worth of loads: the 2,000Wh class.
 LiFePO4 ended the chemistry argument
 Every unit in this comparison is LiFePO4, rated between 1,500 and 4,000 charge cycles. The NMC chemistry that dominated this market until a couple of years ago typically carried ratings under 1,000 cycles, which meant a daily-use unit was measurably worn in two or three years. At 4,000 cycles, using a DELTA 3 every single day would take about 11 years to reach its rated wear point. Even Goal Zero, the last big holdout, moved the Yeti 1000 to LiFePO4 in its 6th generation.
 That means chemistry is no longer a reason to pick one of these over another. It is a reason to be careful with deals: older NMC units are still being cleared out at tempting prices, and the discount is usually not worth the cycle life you give up. The one LiFePO4 caveat that carries over from all lithium: do not charge it below freezing. Bring it inside the rig or tent on cold nights.
 Inverter watts matter less than the ads say
 The inverter rating, 1,500W versus 1,800W versus 2,000W, is the most advertised number and the least likely to affect your trip. A fridge, laptop, lights, fan, and every USB device you own together draw a few hundred watts. Any unit in this group runs all of it at once.
 The inverter number only decides things for heat: kettles, induction burners, hair dryers, microwaves. And there, run the other math first. A 1,500W draw empties a 1,000Wh battery in about 40 minutes, so a big inverter on a small battery mostly buys you the ability to drain it fast. Also read the boosted figures skeptically: EcoFlow's X-Boost (2,200W on the DELTA 3 Plus), Bluetti's Power Lifting (2,700W on the AC180), and Anker's SurgePad are for resistive heating loads only, not motors or compressors. Treat the continuous rating as the real number for anything that spins.
 Charge speed is the real generational change
 This is where the current units genuinely beat what came before. The DELTA 3 and DELTA 3 Plus publish 0-100% in 56 minutes from a stated 1,500W input. The Anker C1000 hits 80% in 43 minutes. The Yeti 1000 takes 1.2 hours, the Bluetti AC180 about 1.3 to 1.8 hours. For camping this matters more than it sounds: a full refill now fits inside a grocery run, a laundromat stop, or lunch in town, which used to require an overnight hookup.
 One transparency note. EcoFlow, Bluetti, Anker, and Goal Zero publish the input wattage behind their claims. Jackery publishes only the time: 1.7 hours for the Explorer 1000 v2, or 1 hour in the app's Emergency Charge mode, with no stated input wattage to check it against. The times may well be accurate.  The Jackery 2000 v2 is the best power station for those who need additional power for multi-day off-grid camping, or for an extended blackout. Recently reduced in price, it can now be found for under $900 on Amazon.  The best value power station for most people is the Anker C1000 Gen 2 . It delivers on most people's basic needs, such as getting through a blackout in comfort, providing power for an off-grid camping trip, or offering portable power away from a 110V outlet. Affordably priced — currently on sale for under $530 — it offers a combination of price, power, and portability that hits the sweet spot: ample power without breaking the bank. 
 If your primary goal is home backup power, step up to the EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 . It is designed specifically for home backup power use, and can be wired directly into your home breaker panel with an optional transfer switch kit. It has an impressive 4.0 kWh power capacity, which can be expanded to up to 48 kWh. 
 After considering more than 40 models, we purchased and tested today's top 14 power stations. Our extensive side-by-side tests measured the runtime delivered with everything from home appliances to camping gear.  The Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 offers ample power to support multi-day off-grid camping needs and allow you to stay comfortable during an extended blackout. It delivers quiet operation and is relatively easy to tote around at 39 lbs. It offers an impressive 2,042 Wh capacity, of which we measured 1,710 Wh available as usable AC power output. Solar panels are an easy-to-use option to extend the v2's capacity, and Jackery solar panels are well-made and extremely easy to use. For those with existing non-Jackery-branded solar panels, buying an adapter cable is required (about $25 on Amazon). Despite these minor drawbacks, the Jackery 2000 v2 remains our top choice for providing ample power for multi-day off-grid adventures.

 How We Tested
 Our testing process for power stations is extensive. We subject each product to hundreds of hours of hands-on use and testing to evaluate power output, runtime, device compatibility, and ease of operation. 
 We do not rely on manufacturer claims or specifications to determine things like each product's actual usable AC power output. We use sophisticated power measurement equipment, along with some creative test jigs of our own custom design, to stress test each product and measure its real-world capabilities. 
 None of the products we tested actually delivers usable AC power output that matches their claimed capacity . For example, a 2,000 watt-hour power station will not provide you with 2,000 watt-hours of usable AC power — only 60% to 93% of the claimed capacity is actually delivered and usable to power your devices through the AC outlets. Since products vary so widely in the actual usable power they deliver, we consider the usable AC power output to be the single most important information to help guide your purchase decision-making. 
 We use precision power measurement equipment to measure runtime and charging speeds. You can learn more about our power station testing protocol and process, in our How We Test article.

 What's the Best Value?
 The Jackery 300 is the winner of our Best Buy award because it is small, affordable, and a great solution for keeping your phone and laptop recharged. However, it won't be a great value if your goal is to power higher-wattage devices or appliances — for example, you can't power a space heater, stove burner, or even a hot water kettle with the Jackery 300. 
 Figure out how much power you need . From our perspective, the best value strategy for power stations is to focus on what you want to power and avoid overspending on more capacity than you actually need. 
 Choosing the right power station is largely determined by your power needs. To save money, first figure out how much power you need, then pick the best device that meets your needs.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 While it is tempting to jump to higher power output, keep in mind that doubling power capacity will double the cost (and the weight). It might not be worth it. (Although we admittedly find ourselves wanting more power now for off-grid camping than we did in the past.)
 Adding Solar Can Save You Money 
A 2,000 Wh power station like the Jackery 2000 v2 might be all the power you need for a weekend camping trip. But you are unlikely to get 5-7 days of off-grid camping power out of it. Going to a 4,000 Wh power station could solve that problem, but it will cost you another $1,000 . A more economical solution? Consider adding a 200 watt solar panel for less than $400 , which might extend your runtime for days.
 The good news is costs are coming down . Unlike most consumer electronics categories, power stations and solar panels have become much more affordable over the last few years. In 2024, each 1,000 Wh of power station capacity would cost you about $1,000, or $1/Wh. Today, many of the most compelling power station products can be found for less than half that cost — around $0.40/Wh.

But in practice, most of these Specialty features are not required. We feel the ability to expand the battery capacity is the only specialty feature that deserves significant consideration in your purchase decision; you may find, as we do ourselves, that you desire more power capacity down the road than you calculate you need today. 
 Does a Power Station make a good UPS? Some power stations offer the ability to work as an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) which can continue to power a device like a Desktop Computer in the event of a power outage. While this sounds like a nifty feature, in practice using a $1,500 Power Station to back up a desktop computer is a waste of money compared to a buying a quality $200 APC or CyberPower UPS, which work better, offer more features, and are a lot less expensive. If this feature comes with the power station you buy that is a plus — but we consider it a nice-to-have feature, not a requirement. For those who are really looking for a UPS system for something like a Desktop Computer, we'd recommend shopping for one separately rather using a power station for that purpose.

 Considering all of the above factors, with more weight placed on the basic features, here is how we rated the products on Features:
 How to Choose A Power Station
 Before deciding which power station will be right for you, there are a few key factors to consider. Below are some key questions that summarize key points from our buying advice article.
 An electric cooler is very convenient for camping. But, be sure to bring it to a cool temperature at home or when plugged into your car 12v plug while driving, since the initial cooling is when it draws the most power.   Credit: Matt Lighthart 
 How Much Power Do I Need? 
 Power stations are more limited in the maximum AC wattage and runtime they can provide, which is intuitively obvious. We are all accustomed to plugging in whatever we want into an AC outlet, and it just works. But, off-grid camping power or managing through a multi-day blackout requires planning about what kinds of devices you run to avoid fully depleting your power station prematurely. Dialing in your power station requirements takes discipline: you may need to pull back from what you want , to think about what you really need . 
 The Power Output section above includes some tables to help you determine what power station capacity will best meet your requirements.
 Note that certain kinds of devices, like space heaters, cooking appliances, and charging ebikes, are much more demanding of power than most other common devices. If you desire to run these higher-power devices, you'll want to calculate your power needs more carefully to ensure you have capacity for the runtime you need. 
 For multi-day power needs, adding optional solar panels may be helpful. Read on below for more info on solar panels.
One of our Editors has invested in a large-scale solar panel system for his home, with 45 solar panels on his roof, and an integrated power station battery capacity of 20 kWh. He notes, “ Our home puts more power into the grid each year than we use, and the power station batteries allow us to pull power when needed during lower-rate cost times of the day. And, we push power onto the grid in the summer during the highest rate for reimbursement times of day. ” Yet, even with that large-scale home backup system, it does not provide enough power for a 24-hour power outage during winter unless he turns off the breakers for all non-essential circuits. The reality is that providing the daily power most on-grid homeowners are accustomed to is beyond the capability of most solar + power station systems.
 What's Your Favorite Electric Gear for Off-grid Camping? 
 We are unabashed fans of electric camping . It can take a yeoman camping trip in the middle of nowhere and turn it into a magical romantic experience or a family fun adventure everyone will remember for years to come. Here's a list of some of our favorite gear and their power requirements:
 LED String Lights — ok, we've got to start with this, because whether it is romance, or a magical family experience, it is all about the lighting . For less than $20 for our best buy winner in string lights , which consumes less than 30 watts of power, you can dress up your campsite with 25 warm glowing LED lights. Oooh. So nice. We love it! And, learn how to play guitar too (acoustic, please) for the full monte. 
 Electric Cooler — we started reviewing electric coolers years ago, but only recently have they become truly awesome. Skip that stop at the store to buy ice, skip all the space taken by the ice, and eliminate the yucky pool of melted water getting in your food on Sunday morning — welcome to the new core tool for camping: the electric cooler. It is a game changer. Pro tip: extend your power station runtime by cooling down your electric cooler using AC power at home, or on the drive plugged into your car 12v plug --it is when cooling down that a powered cooler requires the most electricity. 
 Outdoor Projector — yeah, that is a thing too. Family camping experience: check! Remote location: check! Pixar movie at your campsite: coolest parents ever ! But, do have your power station handy and not fully drained. A quality outdoor projector like the XGIMI Halo+ is a great choice and has its own battery, but if that battery runs out 10 mins before the movie ends, you will go from coolest parents ever to a total meltdown — the power station might save the day (and let you watch more than one movie too)! 
 LED Lanterns — while there may be some who have nostalgia for old-school kerosene or white gas mantel lanterns, at GearLab we love modern LED Lanterns for safe and quiet task lighting when preparing meals. Even if you have a full set of LED String lights, it is great to have a bright rechargeable LED Lantern (or two) when preparing meals or putting a band-aid on a kiddo. 
 Induction Electric Burner — not everyone is ready to give up their old-school fuel-based Coleman camping stove, but we think they are going away in the future too. The full electric camping experience embraces an induction burner (1800W) to replace old-school propane and white gas camping stoves (note you'll need induction-compatible pots and pans to go with it). An induction burner is safer when camping with kids, more efficient with power usage than an old-school electric burner, and you'll rid yourself of the fuel, the fumes, and the fire risks associated with an old-school fuel camping stove . 
 Electric Kettle — boiling water is a recurring task when camping, whether it's for coffee, tea, oatmeal, hot chocolate, or instant “ just-add-water ” foods. A basic electric kettle (1500W) just makes it so easy and fast. 
 Electric Griddle — Another slick addition to your electric camping dream set-up is an electric griddle (1500W). They are great for cooking pancakes, eggs, grilled cheese sandwiches, bacon, sausage links, and more. 
Keep in mind the power you'll need, which adds up fast. You'll want at least a 2,000 Wh power station, and one with at least 2,000 AC watt support. The cooking devices are high AC Watt so you'll need to run them one at a time unless you buy a higher capacity power station. We love having all three — a kettle , an induction burner , and a griddle — but if space is tight, a burner alone will do. Adding one or two 200 watt solar panels will greatly extend your battery runtime by recharging your power station on sunny days.
 Are Solar Panel(s) a Must-have for a Power Station? 
 No. Many people do not need to invest in solar panels for their power station . The only reason to consider a solar panel is if you need more power over multiple days than your power station can provide. For most people, a suitable power station, like the Jackery 2000 v2 will provide you with adequate power for comfort during a multi-hour blackout and/or a typical weekend camping trip. Obtaining a 12v car adapter charging cable for your power station is a low-cost way to recharge anytime you use your vehicle when camping. 
 In our experience, it is when you need support for 3 or more days without grid power that a solar panel becomes a necessity. 
 A 3-day weekend off-grid camping trip can easily drain your power station and leave you with no power halfway into your trip. 
For example, we recently did a 3-day family camping trip in the Sierra Nevada mountain range using the Jackery 2000 v2. Our off-grid campsite included amenities such as LED string lights, an electric cooler, an inductive stove, two ebikes, recharging phones and iPads, and a SpaceX Starlink system. That camp setup draws too much power each day to make it through a 3-day trip. But, by using two 200 watt solar panels, we were able to fully charge up each day. One tester said, “ It was liberating to camp off-grid, in the middle of nowhere, and with such a cool camp setup. My family had a blast! In fact, we had plenty of power to be out there for a week or more of off-grid camping, so long as the sun kept shining .”
 What Size Solar Panel to Get for a Power Station? 
 If you want to add solar panels for a power station with a battery capacity in the range of 1,000 Wh to 3,000 Wh, we recommend starting with a 200-watt solar panel, which is a good size for most power stations and sells for less than $400. If that is insufficient, consider adding a second 200-watt panel, which will meet the needs of most people for extended off-grid camping or power blackouts.
 Solar Panel Charging Time Estimates
The amount of time it takes a solar panel to charge your power station will depend on the weather, the size of the solar panel, the efficiency of the solar panel at charging, whether you just need to top off charge to 100% or fully charge from 0%, and lastly, the watt-hour capacity of your power station. Our tests of solar panels reveal the following rules of thumb, which we've used in the table below:
 4-6 hours of peak sun a day — a good rule of thumb is that you can get 4-6 hours of peak sun charging on a clear, sunny day. Your mileage may vary, but in our experience, those are good numbers for planning your power on an off-grid camping adventure. 
 80% solar charging efficiency — we've extensively tested solar panels for charging efficiency , and the results vary widely, from as low as 50% to as high as 90% efficiency. For our calculations in the table below, we assume 80% efficiency based on the results of testing of the better quality 200 watt solar panels. 
 200-watt solar panels for most people — We consider the 200-watt solar panel to be the sweet spot for most people with power stations in the popular size of 1,000 Wh to 2,000 Wh. The 200 watt size packs well, and there is a lot of competition, which means you can get a quality panel for a good price.

 As you can see in the table above, a 100-watt solar panel is the only option for a low-end power station in the 300 watt or lower capacity, and we consider 100 watt solar panels impractical for any power station with a capacity of 1,000 Wh or higher. We recommend 200-watt panel(s) as the right solution for 1,000 Wh to 2,000 Wh capacity range. A typical need is just to top off your charge each day (rather than providing 100% full recharge), and for that scenario a single 200-watt panel will likely do the job. If you find you need more solar charging, then add a second 200-watt panel. The GearLab team often brings (2) x 200-watt solar panels for our off-grid camping, using a 2,000 Wh power station, since we tend to be more aggressive in our power utilization, using higher-demand devices like electric cooking stovetops and ebike charging.

 Other Notable Power Stations
 Competition is high among power station manufacturers, offering consumers a wide range of options to choose from. Below are some of the notable options available, with our thoughts on each.
 Jackery HomePower 3000 — The 3000 is the logical step up from the Jackery 2000 v2. It includes all the features we love about the 2000 v2, but with 50% more power. It sells for around $1,200, about $400 more than the Jackery 2000 v2. For that extra $400, you get a significant upgrade in power output, including (1) 30amp AC outlet and (4) 20 amp AC outlets (the 2000 v2 maxes out at 18 amps), and a 3,072 Wh capacity (about 50% more than the 2000 v2's 2,042 Wh). The maximum watts is similarly increased to 3,600 watt max versus the 2000 v2's 2,200 watt max. That added power gives you about 50% more runtime and an enhanced ability to power large home appliances during blackouts, as well as high-power tools like circular saws and table saws. It weighs 60 lbs, which is at the high end of what is manageable for use camping, but if you are OK with that weight, it can serve well for off-grid camping adventures as well as home backup power. For those who need more power output than the Jackery 2000 v2 can deliver, the 3000 is a high-quality upgrade worth considering. 
 Ecoflow Trail 300 — the Trail 300 is a uniquely designed DC-only small power station that sells for about $150 and provides 288Wh of capacity in a compact and lightweight vertical format. It is small enough to fit in a backpack, but it offers no AC outlets — just (4) USB ports and a 12V car socket. It weighs 6 lbs and is intended for the user who wants to hike into a remote location with ample power to recharge phones and laptops. We consider it an innovative, but niche solution that uniquely addresses a need we think few people have. For hiking into a remote location, power banks are much smaller and lighter, and make for a better backpack-friendly solution. And, if you are car camping, a product like the Jackery 300 is sufficiently small and light, but offers much more capability, including (2) AC outlets, and costs only $30 more.
 Jackery Explorer 300D — similar to the Ecoflow Trail 300 noted above, the 300D is lightweight, small enough to fit in a backpack, and offers only USB power ( DC-only , no AC outlets). It weighs about 5 lbs and offers 288Wh of claimed capacity. It is marketed for a niche audience who will take it backpacking or hiking, and yet need more power than smaller, lighter and much more convenient power banks , or better yet, a solar power bank product provides. The 300D is a unique solution. But, quite frankly, we consider the 300D, like the Ecoflow 300 noted above, as niche solutions that answer a question not many people are asking. 
 Pecron E2000LFP — Pecron is a manufacturer of power stations based in China whose products are about 20% less expensive in terms of dollars per Wh capacity. Despite the low prices, we don't recommend the brand due to concerns we have about reliability. User reviews provide evidence of a significant number of reported product failures and warranty returns. Pecron appears to be standing behind the product, and user reviews indicate that they honor their warranty. But, we are left uncomfortable recommending Pecron power stations, despite low street prices. 
 Ecoflow Delta Pro Ultra X — for those who are looking for a robust whole home backup power solution, the Ultra X delivers big power capacity, 12kWh capacity in the base model, which sells for around $8,000, and expandable to a stunning 180kWh capacity. Combined with Ecoflow's Smart Home Panel 3 , the Ultra X can kick in automatically in the event of an outage, so your lights stay on uninterrupted. While offering impressive power, we think the plug-and-play form of the Ultra X is only half the solution. It is expensive, and if you are investing $10k to $20k in this level of power capacity, you will be smart to combine it with rooftop solar panels. A fully integrated solar + battery power solution will require that you obtain a permit from your electrical utility provider so you can sell excess your solar electricity to your power company and draw power from the grid during lower-cost times of day. This class of integrated solar + battery power solutions can deliver significant long-term economic benefits as well as qualify for tax incentives. But, they are not DIY solutions, and you'll need the help of an authorized installer and electrician to put it all together and obtain the necessary permits. If you are interested in this class of solution, we encourage you to solicit competitive bids from reputable solar installers in your area to get a better sense of your options before making a big investment in something like Ecoflow's Ultra X. 
 Bluetti Elite 30 V2 — The Elite 30 V2 is a small form power station intended for device charging and small appliance use. It offers 288 Wh and weighs 9.5 lbs. It works well for small tasks like charging devices and running small appliances, but there are more compelling options in the 200-300 Wh class. 
 Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus — The 5000 Plus sports a 5040 Wh capacity, ideal for powering large home appliances during blackouts, with 240V outlet configurations and expansion options capable of supplying multiple days of backup power. A power station this size is a significant investment and is most practical when integrated with your home's circuits via a transfer switch kit, along with solar panels and additional battery packs, which quickly increases the cost and benefit of owning a power station over a gas generator. 
 Jackery Explorer 500 — The Jackery Explorer 500 shares many of the same qualities as the smaller Jackery 300 but with a bigger battery capacity and higher power output. Though it takes over 5 hours to recharge via a standard wall outlet and has only a single AC port, making it less practical for anything beyond charging phones and laptops. 
 Goal Zero Yeti 500 — The Yeti 500 is a 499 Wh power station that weighs 16 lbs and produces 500 watts of power output. The Yeti 500 has enough power to run some appliances, such as a CPAP machine, but is underpowered for larger items like coffee makers and induction cooktops. Given the limited ports, like only having 2 AC outlets and just one 60 watt USb-C port, there are more enticing options available in the 500 Wh category. 
 DJI Power 2000 — The Power 2000 is DJI's debut in the power station market. It's large enough to cover multiple days of camping or keep an appliance or two charged during an outage. It has a couple of enticing features, such as a 30A RV plug and eight USB-C/USB-A ports. However, the proprietary charging ports are disappointing; you'll need to purchase additional accessories for solar or car charging, quickly making the 2000 an expensive option, especially compared to almost every competitor that has built-in solar and car charging ports. 
 EcoFlow Delta 3 Max — The Delta 3 Max is a beefed up version of the popular EcoFlow Delta 3 . It has double the battery capacity at 2048 Wh and a power output of 2400 watts. The tradeoff is that it weighs 44 lbs and costs a few hundred dollars more than the Delta 3. If you like the Delta lineup but need a bit more capability and battery storage, the Delta 3 Max is worth considering. 
 Anker Solix F3800 — The F3800 is a large, home backup power station that serves as a starting point for building out a full-scale home backup system. It has expandability up to 53.8 kWh, enough to power your home for multiple days during outages. The dual 120V/240V outlet opens up more appliance options, such as clothes dryers and electric ranges, and it also directly supports EV charging via the NEMA 14-50 port. Like any other large, home backup power station, the F3800 is a significant investment and is difficult to transport or move. 
 Conclusion
 Our breakdown of portable power stations aims to simplify the confusing and continually evolving information involved in purchasing one. After months of extensive testing and research, we hope our portable power station review provides the necessary knowledge and guidance to help you make an informed decision about your power needs.
